[0m[38;2;255;255;255m⏺ [0m  Most gardens show how they really work only after a dry month. Planting plans describe
  tidy beds where every plant gets the light it needs, and every row has a clear purpose.

    The second lesson is usually about soil. Nearly every failed bed follows a shortcut: a
  missed compost layer, a packed path, a drain that clogs quietly for months until the
  roots finally rot.
  
  [0m[2m▎[0m [0m[3mIndented one level, a short aside: "simple" and "easy" are not the same. A simple bed [0m
  [0m[2m▎ [0m[3mhas few kinds of plants and clear edges, and keeping it that way often takes real [0m
  [0m[2m▎ [0m[3meffort.[0m
  [0m[2m▎[0m
  [0m[2m▎[0m [0m[2m[3m▎[0m[3m Indented two levels: this is why small plots pay off. Every extra bed, path, or [0m
  [0m[2m▎ [0m[3mtrellis added "just in case" becomes something a future gardener has to weed, water, [0m
  [0m[2m▎ [0m[3mand eventually remove.[0m

    Watering is the part new gardeners most often underestimate. During a heat wave, one
  person needs to water the beds and another needs to watch the forecast: tell the
  neighbors what's happening, what's known, what isn't, and when the next rain will come.
  When the same person does both, both jobs suffer. The waterer gets interrupted
  constantly, and the updates come late, vague, or overconfident.

    The useful habits tend to look like this:
 
  - Water early in the morning, before the sun is high and the leaves can burn.
  - Soak the roots, not the leaves, so the water reaches where it is needed.
  - Mulch the beds in spring, while the soil still holds the winter rain.

    The review at the end of the season is where the real value lies, and it's also the
  step most likely to turn into a chore. A good review doesn't look for a plant to blame.
  It asks why the bed made the mistake easy to make and the problem hard to see.
